accuracy.reason: Server-and-relations and innodb-engine scope the server and engine correctly. Declared-data-rules and transactions-and-durability capture SQL mode, CHECK/null handling, autocommit and default redo flushing without asserting universal safety.

evidence.quote: Several successful SQL statements are not automatically one atomic operation.

mechanisms.reason: Isolation-and-locking distinguishes snapshot from current locking reads and explains wait/deadlock retry. Clustered-indexes links primary-key width to secondary entries; replication-limits and backups-and-recovery separate receipt, application, local recovery and historical replay.

evidence.quote: Locking reads and writes use different current-data rules from snapshot reads, and locks may cover index ranges.

coherence.reason: All nine objectives build from server/engine through schema, transaction/isolation, indexes and recovery to a scoped choice. Prerequisites suffice. Assigned diagrams match engine boundary, secondary lookup and backup/log replay; shared assets inspected without runtime rendering.

evidence.quote: Crash recovery uses engine recovery information to restore local transactional consistency after a crash.

decisions.reason: Requirement-led-choice includes connections, transaction duration, read/write traffic, freshness, loss and downtime. Guarantees and index benefits are conditional, with replica write limits and deployment alternatives retained.

evidence.quote: Clarify read/write traffic, stale-read tolerance, acknowledged-write loss, write latency and downtime.

clarity.reason: Examples demonstrate SQL-mode conversion and repeatable snapshots, and all major terms are defined before use. Precise boundaries prevent transferring guarantees to other engines or external actions.

evidence.quote: Know which engine your tables use before relying on its guarantees.

outcomes.reason: All six criteria supported: SQL server and shared relational clients, application design responsibilities, storage engine role, InnoDB-specific features and surviving contention despite finer locks.

All eight criteria supported: types and key/null rules, required nonnegative/reference choices, version/mode enforcement, application-invariant limits, explicit transaction versus autocommit, ACID scope and redo durability, external HTTP exclusion.

All eight criteria supported: row versions/isolation, first ordinary-read snapshot and current locking distinction, safe FOR UPDATE/check/change transaction with no allocation on failure, whole deadlock retry, clustered/secondary layout and key width, conditional key choice and measured plans/costs.

All eight criteria supported: binlog receive/apply and lag, async loss risk, freshness routing and promotion authority, separate crash/failover/history roles, copied deletion, compatible base plus continuous logs to stop point, retention and tested usable restoration.

All four criteria supported: conditional engine/schema fit, transaction controls/retry and measured key/index design, stale-aware replicas with source-write limits and bounded connections, clarified traffic/failure targets and tested recovery responsibilities.

sourceChecks.claim: Live MySQL overview confirms relational SQL and client/server architecture with multiple client programs and libraries; lesson accurately describes the ordinary server deployment.
Live InnoDB introduction identifies it as default, with ACID/crash recovery, row-level locking and foreign keys. Transaction page distinguishes nontransactional engines.
Live SQL Modes gives the exact invalid integer conversion versus strict rejection example. CHECK Constraints followup confirms false fails while UNKNOWN passes, and enforcement can be configured.
Live COMMIT documentation defines START TRANSACTION, commit/rollback and default autocommit. InnoDB parameter followup confirms default redo flush at each commit and crash-loss risk when relaxed.

Live isolation page verifies first-read Repeatable Read snapshots and distinct locking rules. Locking Reads followup verifies FOR UPDATE reads current data and locks; Deadlocks Handling requires retrying aborted transactions and keeping them short.

Live clustered-index page says row data resides in the clustered index and secondary records contain primary-key columns; long keys increase secondary space. Query-based planning remains a conditional recommendation.

Live replication chapter identifies asynchronous source-to-replica copying. Previously checked GTID function documentation distinguishes applied transactions and timeout, substantiating freshness progress checks; lost unpropagated writes follow the stated async boundary.

Live point-in-time recovery page explicitly starts with full backup and advances with later changes; its binary-log recovery section provides the retained-history mechanism. The lesson correctly rejects logs without a compatible base.

Live InnoDB introduction establishes shared transactional features; checked isolation, indexing, replication and recovery documentation supports the stated contention, freshness and operating costs. This is a requirements synthesis, not a capacity promise.
